← Walk-in shower bid calculator

How much to charge to install a walk-in shower

The number a homeowner wants is a price per square foot of tile. That number is not a takeoff. A 5x3 alcove tub-to-shower with the existing valve is not the same job as a 5x5 curbless walk-in with a linear drain and frameless glass. The tile count is close. The hours are not.

Open the free bid calculator

Count the drain and the glass, not just the tile

Flooring calculators price LVP, hardwood, and floor tile with a waste factor. Cabinet and countertop calculators price kitchens. Drywall prices hang-and-finish. A walk-in shower is a wet-area system: tear-out, a valve that may move, waterproofing, wall and floor tile, niches, a bench, and glass. Quoting all of that from a published per-square-foot number is how the first linear drain eats the field margin.

A shower with similar tile can cost much more

Each curbless floor is extra slope and extra waterproofing that never appears in the wall count. A linear drain is billed as its own hours and its own kit. A valve relocate and a masonry bench are adders that get forgotten on a brochure special. On the sample rates a 5x5 curbless walk-in with a linear drain, valve relocate, two niches, a masonry bench, and frameless glass prices about $12,821 ($111 per tile sq ft, 55.4 crew-hours). The same shop’s 5x3 alcove tub-to-shower with a framed door prices about $7,419 ($78 per tile sq ft, 29.0 hours, walk-away $5,341). Matching the brochure job’s per-square-foot number on the walk-in is how that job becomes a loss. See should I match an alcove price on a curbless walk-in.

Steam and tile-only are not a markup on the alcove

A steam shower is not an alcove plus 20%. On the sample rates a 4x6 steam job with a masonry bench, two niches, and a steam-rated enclosure prices about $15,441 ($115 per tile sq ft, 51.0 crew-hours) — more money than the walk-in, not because there is more tile but because the generator and the sealed glass do not live in a published per-SF number. A tile-only alcove with the demo already done and no glass prices about $5,637 (25.0 hours). Treating either as a blended add-on is how the special that looked fine turns into a loss after the first steam leak path.

Load the wage, then keep a walk-away number

A $38/h setter loaded at 32% payroll burden is $50.16. Margin is a share of the price you send, not a markup on cost. The walk-away price is total cost — below that the job makes nothing before you take a dollar home. Replace every rate with your invoices before you send either number.

Customer-supplied tile is not a free set

Owners also shop a second special: “I already bought the tile — just set it for $45 / SF.” Zeroing the tile invoice drops the bid. The set hours stay. Leftover boxes they want back are still hours. A short order or a dye-lot mismatch is a second trip. See should I install customer-supplied tile for the three-way comparison on the same shower.

Saturday is not the weekday bid

Owners also call with a weekday number and ask you to start Saturday so they can keep the only shower. After-hours is time-and-a-half plus a second evening trip — you cannot leave mud overnight. On the sample rates a 5x3 alcove prices about $7,418.51 when they leave and $8,894.37 after hours. A $5,500 Saturday number covers the weekday and loses $903.94. See should I tile a walk-in shower after hours.

What this is not

This is not a plumbing specification, a waterproofing warranty, a building-code determination, a permit, or a recommended market price. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. Slope, drain type, membrane, and whether the valve must move are yours to confirm.

Price your shower

Common questions

How much to charge to install a walk-in shower?

Charge from wall and floor tile, waterproofing, tub tear-out, valve relocate, linear drain, curbless slope, niches, bench, glass, loaded labor, overhead, and a margin that is a share of price. A default 5x3 alcove tub-to-shower at the sample rates in this calculator prices around $7,419 — about $78 per square foot of tile.

Why is a per-square-foot shower quote dangerous?

Homeowners count tile. Linear drains, curbless slope, a valve relocate, niches, a masonry bench, and frameless glass do not scale with that count. Matching a cheaper per-SF quote written for a brochure alcove is how a curbless walk-in becomes a week-long loss.

Does a shower with more tile always cost more to install?

Not in proportion. On the sample rates a 5x5 curbless walk-in with a linear drain, valve relocate, two niches, a masonry bench, and frameless glass prices around $12,821 ($111 per tile sq ft), while a 5x3 alcove tub-to-shower with similar tile prices around $7,419 ($78 per tile sq ft).

      Common questions

      Why does a curbless shower cost so much more than a standard framed one?

      Curbless floors need the subfloor recessed or built up to create a barrier-free slope to the drain, which is a different framing and waterproofing detail than a standard curbed pan — that extra work, plus a linear drain if selected, adds hours a curbed shower never needs.       The customer already bought the tile — does that mean labor is cheap?

      No. Zeroing the tile invoice is not a free set: unpacking, sorting, and setting owner-supplied tile still takes the same hours, and a short order or dye-lot mismatch becomes your second trip and a retail fill-in the customer expects you to cover, not a cost you caused. Price the labor the same way regardless of who bought the material.

      Does relocating the valve or adding a bench get priced automatically from the square footage?

      No, they're separate toggles because they don't scale with tile area — a valve relocate is plumbing work behind the wall, and a masonry bench is its own framed and waterproofed structure, both add fixed hours on top of whatever the wall and floor tile square footage already costs.

← Walk-in shower bid calculator

Should I install customer-supplied tile?

Owners call with boxes in the hallway: “I already bought the tile. Can you just set it for $45 a square foot?” That sounds like free margin because the tile invoice left the bid. It did not leave the set hours, the leftover boxes they want back, or the chance that 95 square feet of takeoff arrived as 80 square feet of one dye lot.

Open the free walk-in shower bid calculator

Zeroing the tile is not a free set

A contractor-supplied alcove still carries the tile invoice. An owner-supplied order that actually covers the takeoff zeros that line and keeps the same set hours, plus unpack and leftover-box handling. On a typical 5x3 alcove tub-to-shower — $38 wage, 32% burden, 16% overhead, 28% target margin — the contractor-supplied bid is about $7,419. Zeroing $8 / SF tile drops it, but the owner-supplied walk-away stays above the $45 / SF labor-only number ($4,275 on 95 SF). Taking the “just set what they bought” special still loses money.

A short order is a second trip

Store shelves and leftover boxes from a kitchen backsplash do not equal a wet-area takeoff plus waste. A dye-lot mismatch on the last wall is a drive back, a retail fill-in, or a wait. Price that callback on the same shower before you agree. The calculator adds a starting second trip and a retail fill-in on top of the rates you already typed.

How to use the comparison

Open the walk-in shower bid calculator, enter the bathroom you are standing in, and put their labor-only number in “price you’re considering” if they named one. The who-supplies table scores $45 / SF of tile — or their number — against you-supply, owner-supplies-it-covers, and owner-supplies-short. Nothing is uploaded.

They want Saturday? See should I tile a walk-in shower after hours. It is not a plumbing specification, a waterproofing warranty, or a reason to refuse a customer — it is the walk-away number on each supply path. A walk-in tub is a tub with a door. A toilet is a commode swap. This prices a wet-area system.

Common questions

Should I install tile the customer bought at a store?

Only after you price the set without the tile invoice. Unpacking their boxes is still a set, leftover boxes they want back are still hours, and a short order or dye-lot mismatch is a second trip. A $45 / SF labor-only special often sits under that walk-away number even when the tile is free to you.

Does customer-supplied tile make the $45 / SF labor-only special profitable?

Usually not. Zeroing an $8 / SF tile invoice drops the bid, but loaded labor, waterproofing, glass, travel, and overhead stay. On a typical 5x3 alcove tub-to-shower the owner-supplied walk-away is still above $45 / SF of tile. A short order or a dye-lot mismatch adds a second trip and a retail fill-in.

What if they bought too little tile or the dye lot does not match?

That is a second dispatch plus a retail fill-in they expect you to eat, or a wait while they reorder. Price that callback on the same shower before you agree to set whatever they stacked in the hallway. The calculator adds a starting callback trip and a retail fill-in on top of your current rates.

This calculator vs. Jobber

Two different shapes: Jobber is an account-based platform for running a tile or remodeling company's whole operation, including scheduling the crew and invoicing the customer once a job is priced. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this walk-in shower cost, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

Jobber is a field service management platform used by home service businesses — remodeling, general contracting, plumbing, and cleaning among them — to run client management and online quoting, scheduling and crew dispatch, invoicing and online payments, and a client-facing hub, tied to one account used on an ongoing basis across every job the company runs. Public research puts its founding in 2011, headquartered in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, and reports it is used by more than 200,000 service professionals. Its own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — home service field service management software, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Jobber appears on this page. ← Walk-In Shower Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. tracking it in a spreadsheet

A tile setter pricing an alcove tub-to-shower, a curbless walk-in, or a steam shower usually ends up with a spreadsheet: a tile line, a waterproofing line, a drain or curbless line if this job has one, a bench and glass line, and a new row whenever the job needs something it did not have last time. Every formula is ordinary arithmetic. Keeping it correct as the scope changes under you is the part that gets skipped when a homeowner needs a number today.

What each approach actually does

A spreadsheet can reproduce every line this calculator prices — wall and floor tile hours and material, tile waste, waterproofing, tub tear-out, a valve relocate, a linear drain, curbless slope, niches, a bench, glass, a steam unit, loaded wage, overhead, and target margin. Building it means writing a formula for each of those and remembering which ones to zero out or add back in when the next job is an alcove instead of a curbless walk-in, or has a steam unit this one did not.

This calculator keeps tile, waterproofing, tub tear-out, valve relocate, drain, curbless slope, niches, bench, and glass on one screen, already wired to the job you are pricing. Checking curbless or a linear drain adds their hours and material immediately — a field you have already hand-edited is left alone, but nothing else silently keeps yesterday's number from the last job. A saved bid that reopens on your next visit, a shareable bid link, and a printable customer proposal with a deposit split and a price-held date are each one click, not a second document to build.

QuestionWhere to answer it

Common questions

Can a spreadsheet price a walk-in shower instead?

Yes. Every line this calculator prices — wall and floor tile hours and material, tile waste, waterproofing, tub tear-out, a valve relocate, a linear drain, curbless slope, niches, a bench, glass, a steam unit, loaded wage, overhead, and target margin — is ordinary arithmetic you can put in a spreadsheet. Building it means setting up formulas for each of those and remembering to update every one of them whenever the scope changes, on a wet-area system where tile square footage alone does not predict the cost.

What does a spreadsheet not do that this calculator does?

Switch between an alcove tub-to-shower, a curbless walk-in, a steam shower, and a tile-only job without rebuilding a formula, so a linear drain or a valve relocate is priced the moment you check the box rather than after you remember to add a row for it. It also turns the same numbers into a printable customer proposal with a deposit split and a price-held date, and a shareable bid link that reopens the exact bid for you or your crew, neither of which a formula cell produces on its own.

Is a spreadsheet ever the better choice?

Yes, when the job has a wrinkle this calculator does not model — a second wet area, a custom niche pattern, or a rate structure this tool's fields cannot represent. A spreadsheet you build yourself can represent any line item you can describe. This calculator trades that flexibility for a form that already has the right fields for one tiled shower, wired together so switching scope does not mean rebuilding the sheet.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. Your bid is saved in this browser's local storage between visits, and a bid link you copy carries those same numbers in the page's URL hash rather than sending anything to a server.
